questions.q: What is generally the right first option to consider for a plain CRUD inbound integration need, before building custom Apex?
options: A custom Apex SOAP web service
Salesforce's standard REST or SOAP API
A Platform Event published from outside Salesforce
A custom Apex REST web service with a hand-rolled response shape
questions.explain: The standard REST/SOAP API already covers CRUD on any object with no custom code, and is immediately documented and supported — it's the right default before reaching for custom Apex.

questions.q: When does a custom Apex REST web service earn its added complexity over the standard REST API?
options: Whenever the caller uses JSON instead of XML
When the requirement needs custom business logic, validation, or a response shape beyond plain record CRUD
Only when more than 100 records are involved
Custom Apex REST is always preferred regardless of requirements
questions.explain: Custom Apex REST is justified specifically when logic beyond plain CRUD is needed; otherwise the standard API is simpler to build and maintain.

questions.q: Which of the following is a legitimate inbound integration channel, even though Platform Events are usually discussed as an outbound mechanism?
options: An external system publishing a platform event into Salesforce via the Pub/Sub API or sObject-based REST API
An external system reading a Named Credential directly
An external system modifying Apex governor limits
An external system generating a WSDL on Salesforce's behalf
questions.explain: An external system can publish a platform event into Salesforce, making event publishing a genuine inbound channel, not only something Salesforce initiates outbound.

questions.q: How does inbound integration flip "who owns the contract" compared to outbound integration?
options: There's no difference — the contract owner is always the external system
In outbound integration Salesforce adapts to the external system's API shape; in inbound integration, Salesforce (the service builder) defines the contract that external callers must conform to
In inbound integration, Salesforce never defines any contract at all
Contract ownership only matters for SOAP integrations
questions.explain: Outbound Salesforce is the client adapting to someone else's API; inbound Salesforce is the server whose contract external callers must match — which is why versioning (Lesson 11) matters specifically for inbound services.

questions.q: A requirement is really about notifying Salesforce that something happened elsewhere, rather than fetching or writing one specific record on demand. What should this suggest, per this lesson?
options: Build a custom Apex SOAP web service regardless of the caller's protocol
Consider having the external system publish a platform event instead of calling a request/response endpoint
Always use the standard REST API's bulk endpoints
This scenario cannot be integrated with Salesforce at all
questions.explain: A notification-shaped requirement often fits an event-driven inbound channel (publishing a platform event) better than a synchronous request/response endpoint.
